title: The Evolution of LLM Inference Engines: How vLLM Changed the Game
body_markdown:
This Article is contributed by:[Amit Sehgal](https://www.linkedin.com/in/imamitsehgal/) *,*[Ankur Singh](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ankursharp/) ,[Rajat Mishra](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mishrarajat91/) ,[Satendra Kumar](https://www.linkedin.com/in/satendrakumar06/)


As ML engineers, we’ve witnessed a remarkable transformation in how we serve large language models over the past few years. What started as a simple challenge of loading models into memory has evolved into a sophisticated orchestration of memory management, batching strategies, and hardware optimisation. Today, I want to walk you through this evolution and explain why vLLM represents a paradigm shift in LLM inference.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


#### The Early Days: Naive Inference (2020–2021)


When GPT-3 arrived in 2020, the inference landscape was remarkably simple — perhaps too simple. Most serving solutions followed a straightforward pattern:


- Load the model into GPU memory
- Process requests one at a time
- Generate tokens sequentially using greedy decoding or basic sampling


The problems were immediately apparent. GPU utilisation hovered around 20–30% because the autoregressive nature of language generation left GPUs idle between token generations. Each request was processed in isolation, wasting valuable compute resources. For a 175B parameter model, you might serve only 1–2 requests per second on an H100 GPU — a throughput that simply didn’t scale with demand.


#### First Generation Solutions: Static Batching (2021–2022)


The industry’s first response was static batching. Frameworks like HuggingFace’s transformers with custom serving wrappers, early versions of TensorRT, and initial attempts at FastAPI-based solutions tried to batch multiple requests together.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


**The improvement was real but limited:**


- GPU utilisation improved to 40–50%
- Throughput increased by 2–3x
- Latency remained reasonable for small batches


**But the constraints were frustrating:**


- All sequences in a batch had to be padded to the same length
- The entire batch was held hostage by the longest sequence
- Varying sequence lengths led to wasted computation on padding tokens
- You had to choose: optimise for throughput (large batches, high latency) or optimise for latency (small batches, low throughput)


We spent weeks tuning batch sizes, only to find that our optimal configuration changed with every shift in traffic patterns. It felt like we were fighting the framework instead of just serving models.


#### The ORCA Breakthrough: Iteration-Level Batching (2022)


Microsoft Research’s ORCA paper introduced a concept that seems obvious in retrospect but was revolutionary at the time: **iteration-level batching** . Instead of batching at the request level, why not batch at the token generation level?


This meant:


- Requests could join a batch at any iteration
- Requests could leave a batch when complete
- No more padding waste
- Dynamic batch sizes that adapt to the actual workload


ORCA reported 10x-100x throughput improvements in some scenarios. The industry took notice, but there was a problem: ORCA was primarily a research prototype, not production-ready software.


#### Enter vLLM: Production-Grade Continuous Batching (2023)


This is where the story gets exciting. The team at UC Berkeley’s Sky Computing Lab (later vLLM team) didn’t just implement continuous batching — they solved the memory bottleneck that was preventing these techniques from reaching their full potential.


#### PagedAttention: The Core Innovation


vLLM’s killer feature is **PagedAttention** , inspired by virtual memory and paging in operating systems. Here’s why it matters:


Traditional inference engines allocate contiguous memory for KV caches up front. For a 13B parameter model with a 2048 token context, you might pre-allocate 2–3GB per request. With static batching of 32 requests, that’s 64–96GB just for KV caches — often exceeding available GPU memory.


vLLM’s PagedAttention breaks the KV cache into fixed-size blocks (typically 16–32 tokens) and manages them like virtual memory pages:


Press enter or click to view image in full size


**The impact is dramatic:**


- Near-zero memory waste (internal fragmentation < 4%)
- Memory sharing for common prompt prefixes
- Dynamic memory allocation that grows with actual usage
- 2–4x higher batch sizes on the same hardware


#### Continuous Batching in Production


vLLM implements continuous batching elegantly:


1. **Preemption and swapping** : When GPU memory is tight, vLLM can preempt low-priority requests, swap their KV cache to CPU, and resume them later
2. **Prefix caching** : Common prompt prefixes are computed once and shared across requests
3. **Speculative decoding support** : Integration with draft models for faster generation
4. **Chunked prefill** : Long prompts are processed in chunks to maintain interactivity


In practice, vLLM can give:


- 10–20x throughput improvement over naive inference
- 2–4x improvement over static batching
- Sub-second time-to-first-token (TTFT) even under load
- Consistent inter-token latency


#### The Ecosystem That Followed


vLLM’s success catalysed the entire ecosystem:


**TensorRT-LLM** (NVIDIA): Adopted continuous batching with in-flight batching, heavily optimised for NVIDIA hardware with custom kernels


**LMDeploy** (MMRazor): Optimised for production deployment with a focus on stability


**SGLang** (Sky Computing Lab): Built on vLLM with structured generation support


The competition has been healthy. Each framework has strengths:


- vLLM: Best memory efficiency, broad compatibility
- TensorRT-LLM: Peak performance on NVIDIA hardware
- SGLang: Best for constrained generation


#### Why vLLM Remains My Go-To


Despite the competition, vLLM remains my default choice for several reasons:


1. **Simplicity** : Python-native, minimal config, works out of the box
2. **Transparency** : Memory usage is predictable and debuggable
3. **Flexibility** : Works with any Transformer model with minimal changes
4. **Community** : Exceptional responsiveness to issues and PRs
5. **Extensibility** : Easy to customise attention mechanisms, sampling, etc.


Here’s how simple it is to get started:


```text
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams  # Initialize the model  llm = LLM(model="meta-llama/Llama-2-70b-hf",            tensor_parallel_size=4,            gpu_memory_utilization=0.95)
```


```text
# Generate responses  prompts = ["Hello, how are you?", "Write a Python function..."]  sampling_params = SamplingParams(temperature=0.8, top_p=0.95)  outputs = llm.generate(prompts, sampling_params)
```


For serving, the OpenAI-compatible API server works beautifully:


```text
python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \      --model meta-llama/Llama-2-70b-hf \      --tensor-parallel-size 4
```


#### Looking Forward: What’s Next?


The inference engine landscape continues to evolve rapidly, and two particularly exciting developments are reshaping how we think about LLM infrastructure at scale:


#### LMCache: Cross-Engine KV Cache Sharing


While AIBrix focuses on system orchestration, **LMCache** tackles a related but distinct problem: efficiently moving KV caches between GPU memory, CPU memory, storage layers, and across different inference engines.


LMCache is a KV cache management layer that’s deeply integrated with vLLM (and SGLang) and has been adopted by the vLLM production stack, KServe, and NVIDIA’s Dynamo framework.


**Why LMCache matters:**


In traditional inference, KV cache lives and dies in GPU memory. If you want to reuse it across queries or transfer it between instances, you’re out of luck. LMCache changes this by:


**Cache Offloading** : Store KV caches in a hierarchy (GPU → CPU DRAM → Local Disk → Remote Storage → Redis) and retrieve them on demand. For RAG applications where you’re repeatedly processing the same document chunks, this is transformative.


**Prefill-Decode Disaggregation** : Separate the prefill phase (processing the prompt) from the decode phase (generating tokens). Run prefill on cheaper GPUs or even CPUs, cache the resulting KV, then transfer it to decode-optimised instances. This architectural separation can maintain consistent decode latency even under variable load.


**Cross-Engine Sharing** : Share KV caches between different vLLM instances or even between vLLM and SGLang. This enables sophisticated deployment patterns where specialised instances handle different workload types.


**Real-world performance is impressive:** 15x throughput improvement on multi-round question answering, 3–10x latency reduction on ShareGPT conversation traces, and the ability to handle context sizes that would otherwise exceed GPU memory.


The beauty of LMCache is its modularity. It’s not a replacement for vLLM — it’s an enhancement layer that plugs in cleanly and provides immediate benefits for long-context and high-reuse scenarios.


#### AIBrix: System-Level Orchestration for Production


While vLLM solved the inference engine problem, deploying it at enterprise scale introduces a new set of challenges: routing, autoscaling, multi-tenancy, and distributed KV cache management. This is where **AIBrix** comes in.


Developed by ByteDance and now part of the vLLM project ecosystem, AIBrix is a Kubernetes-native control plane that sits above vLLM and other inference engines. Think of it as the missing orchestration layer for production LLM deployments.


**What makes AIBrix compelling:**


**Distributed KV Cache** : This is the killer feature. AIBrix enables KV cache sharing across different vLLM instances and even across different nodes. Instead of each vLLM instance maintaining its own isolated KV cache, AIBrix creates a distributed cache pool that all instances can access. The impact? 50% throughput increase and 70% latency reduction in real deployments.


Imagine you’re running a customer support bot. User A starts a conversation on instance 1, but the next message gets routed to instance 2 (maybe instance 1 is overloaded). With traditional vLLM, instance 2 would need to recompute the entire conversation history. With AIBrix’s distributed cache, it simply fetches the cached KV from the pool — no recomputation needed.


**High-Density LoRA Management** : Deploy thousands of LoRA adapters with dynamic loading and intelligent scheduling. AIBrix reported 4.7x cost reduction in low-traffic scenarios by efficiently packing multiple adapters.


**LLM-Aware Routing** : Prefix-aware, load-aware routing that understands which instances have relevant cached prefixes. This isn’t just round-robin load balancing — it’s intelligent routing that maximises cache hits.


**SLO-Driven GPU Optimisation** : Heterogeneous serving that mixes GPU types (A100s, H100s, L40s) while maintaining service level objectives. The system dynamically adjusts allocations based on workload characteristics.


AIBrix represents the maturation of LLM infrastructure from


> how do we serve one model to how do we operate a fleet of models across a data center.


If you’re running vLLM in production at scale, AIBrix should be on your radar.


#### Other Exciting Directions


Beyond AIBrix and LMCache, the field is moving fast:


**Multi-LoRA serving at scale** : Beyond just loading adapters, we’re seeing sophisticated scheduling that predicts which adapters to keep warm based on request patterns.


**Continuous batching for multi-modal models** : Extending PagedAttention and continuous batching to vision-language models, where you’re batching both text tokens and image patches.


**ML-based scheduling** : Using learned models to predict sequence lengths, optimal batch composition, and preemption decisions rather than heuristics.


**Hardware co-design** : Custom accelerators (like Groq’s LPU) designed from the ground up with PagedAttention-style memory management and streaming architectures.


**Speculative decoding improvements** : Better draft models, multi-candidate speculation, and learned acceptance thresholds that adapt to workload characteristics.


The convergence of AIBrix’s orchestration, LMCache’s efficient cache management, and vLLM’s core inference engine creates a complete stack that addresses inference challenges from the GPU kernel level all the way up to data centre-scale deployment. This is what production-grade LLM infrastructure looks like in 2025.

#### Conclusion


The journey from naive inference to vLLM represents one of the most impactful developments in practical ML engineering. PagedAttention and continuous batching aren’t just incremental improvements — they fundamentally changed what’s possible with LLM serving.


As models continue to grow and inference demands increase, the efficiency gains from vLLM translate directly to:


- Lower costs (fewer GPUs needed)
- Better user experience (lower latency)
- Higher throughput (more users served)
- Greater accessibility (smaller teams can serve large models)


The beauty of vLLM is that it makes best practices accessible to everyone. You don’t need a team of GPU kernel engineers to get state-of-the-art inference performance. You just need to understand the concepts and use the right tool.


If you’re still using naive inference or static batching for LLM serving, you’re leaving 5–10x performance on the table. The migration to vLLM is straightforward, and the benefits are immediate and measurable.


The inference engine evolution isn’t over — but vLLM has set a new baseline that every solution will be measured against.
